finalCtaTitle: Choose the Correct Company-Closure Route First
finalCtaDescription: Before you proceed, speak with our experts. Winding up of Companies can directly impact directors, shareholders, creditors, employees, tax records, GST, bank accounts, ROC compliance, licences and future liability. Do not leave a company inactive and assume the risk is over. A short discussion today can help you choose the correct closure route, avoid penalties and complete dissolution with confidence.

blocks.text: Winding up of Companies is the legal process through which a company’s business is brought to an end, its assets are realised, liabilities are settled, remaining surplus is distributed and the company is finally dissolved.

It matters because an improperly closed company can continue to attract ROC notices, tax demands, director disqualification, creditor claims, bank account issues, GST non-compliance, litigation, penalty exposure and future due diligence problems.

This service is relevant for companies that cannot continue business, companies facing shareholder deadlock, fraudulent or non-compliant companies, companies with long-pending filings, group entities being closed, solvent companies seeking voluntary liquidation, creditors seeking recovery, and promoters who want a legally clean closure route.
Winding up of Companies is not a licence. It is a statutory legal process for liquidation and dissolution of a company.

It is regulated by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs, Registrar of Companies, National Company Law Tribunal, Official Liquidator / Company Liquidator, IBBI, and other authorities depending on the closure route.

It is not mandatory for every company closure. For inactive companies, strike-off may be possible; for solvent companies, voluntary liquidation may be used; for Tribunal-based winding up, NCLT process applies.
In simple terms…
Winding up means legally closing the company after collecting assets, paying liabilities and completing formal dissolution.
The company does not disappear merely because business has stopped. Until it is struck off, liquidated or dissolved through proper legal process, it continues to exist in statutory records.
From a compliance perspective…

Winding up of Companies requires closure-route selection, board and shareholder review, debt and asset assessment, creditor position, statutory filing status, tax compliance, employee dues, bank closure, NCLT/IBC/ROC procedure, liquidator appointment, public notices, claim settlement and final dissolution documentation.
From a risk perspective, the first question should always be: Is winding up the correct route, or should the company use strike-off or voluntary liquidation?

faqs.q: What is Winding up of Companies?
faqs.a: Winding up of Companies is the legal process of closing a company by realising assets, settling liabilities and dissolving the entity.

faqs.q: Is Winding up of Companies a licence?
faqs.a: No. It is not a licence. It is a legal closure, liquidation and dissolution process.

faqs.q: Who regulates winding up of companies?
faqs.a: MCA, ROC, NCLT, Official Liquidator, Company Liquidator, IBBI and sector regulators may be involved depending on the route.

faqs.q: Which law applies to winding up?
faqs.a: The Companies Act, 2013, Companies (Winding Up) Rules, 2020 and IBC, 2016 may apply depending on the closure route.

faqs.q: Which section deals with winding up by Tribunal?
faqs.a: Section 271 of the Companies Act, 2013 deals with circumstances where a company may be wound up by Tribunal.

faqs.q: Who can file winding-up petition?
faqs.a: The company, contributory, Registrar, authorised person, Central Government or State Government may file in specified circumstances.

faqs.q: Is inability to pay debts still a Companies Act winding-up ground?
faqs.a: Debt insolvency issues are generally dealt with under IBC. Current company-law winding-up grounds under Section 271 should be reviewed carefully before filing.

faqs.q: What is the difference between winding up and strike-off?
faqs.a: Winding up is a liquidation process, generally involving Tribunal/liquidator. Strike-off is ROC removal of name for eligible inactive companies.

faqs.q: What is voluntary liquidation?
faqs.a: Voluntary liquidation is an IBC Section 59 process for solvent corporate persons that can pay debts fully and want formal liquidation.

faqs.q: Can an active company apply for strike-off?
faqs.a: Strike-off eligibility must be reviewed carefully. Active companies with business, assets, liabilities or disputes may not be suitable for strike-off.

faqs.q: What is NCLT’s role in winding up?
faqs.a: NCLT hears winding-up petitions, appoints liquidator, supervises process and orders final dissolution.

faqs.q: What is the role of Company Liquidator?
faqs.a: The liquidator takes control of assets, reviews affairs, invites claims, realises assets, pays liabilities and applies for dissolution.

faqs.q: Can a company be wound up for five years of filing default?
faqs.a: Yes. Default in filing financial statements or annual returns for five consecutive financial years is a statutory ground.

faqs.q: Can shareholders decide to wind up a company?
faqs.a: Shareholders may pass a special resolution, but the correct legal route and Tribunal/IBC/ROC process must be followed.

faqs.q: Can creditors object to company closure?
faqs.a: Yes. Creditors may object if liabilities are unpaid or closure affects their rights.

faqs.q: Can directors be liable after winding up?
faqs.a: Directors may face liability for fraud, misfeasance, unpaid statutory dues, false declarations or non-compliance depending on facts.

faqs.q: What happens to company assets?
faqs.a: Assets are realised or transferred according to law, and proceeds are used to settle liabilities before surplus distribution.

faqs.q: What happens to employees?
faqs.a: Employee dues, salary, gratuity, PF, ESIC and labour obligations must be reviewed and settled as per applicable law.

faqs.q: What happens to pending court cases?
faqs.a: Proceedings may require Tribunal leave or appropriate legal handling depending on the stage and type of winding up.

faqs.q: Can GST registration continue after company closure?
faqs.a: No. GST registration should be cancelled or closed through proper process where applicable.

faqs.q: Can bank account remain open after closure?
faqs.a: Bank accounts should be closed or handled as per liquidator/closure requirements before final dissolution.

faqs.q: Can a regulated company be wound up normally?
faqs.a: Regulated entities may require regulator approval, intimation or licence surrender before closure.

faqs.q: How long does winding up take?
faqs.a: Timeline depends on route, filings, assets, liabilities, creditors, litigation, liquidator process, NCLT workload and regulator involvement.

faqs.q: What is the biggest mistake in company closure?
faqs.a: The biggest mistake is choosing strike-off, winding up or voluntary liquidation without first checking assets, liabilities, filings, taxes, charges, creditors and regulator obligations.

faqs.q: Can Estabizz handle complete winding-up support?
faqs.a: Yes. Estabizz assists with closure-route assessment, documentation, NCLT/ROC/IBC support, tax/GST closure, liquidator coordination and final dissolution tracking.
